title: Connectionless Datagrams, Message Boundaries & TCP vs. UDP
topic: Connectionless Transport, UDP Headers, Datagram Boundaries, Ports, TCP vs. UDP
learning_objectives: Observe connectionless UDP socket calls (socket SOCK_DGRAM, bind, sendto, recvfrom, close) with no handshake.
Verify that UDP preserves discrete application datagram boundaries across varied payload sizes.
Compare UDP behavior against TCP when the server is unavailable.

concept_explanation.title: Connectionless Transport & Minimal 8-Byte Header
concept_explanation.summary: UDP provides best-effort, message-oriented delivery with only an 8-byte header (source port, destination port, length, checksum). There is no handshake, no sequence tracking, and no retransmission.
key_points: A UDP server does NOT call listen() or accept(); it binds and loops on recvfrom()/sendto().
Each sendto() transmits one discrete datagram; each recvfrom() receives one discrete datagram (message boundaries are preserved).

concept_explanation.title: TCP vs. UDP Trade-Offs
concept_explanation.summary: TCP prioritizes ordered, reliable byte streams; UDP prioritizes low latency and minimal overhead for protocols like DNS, VoIP, QUIC, and telemetry.
key_points: Sending a UDP datagram to an unbound port succeeds locally at sendto() — the client only discovers unavailability via timeout or ICMP Port Unreachable.
UDP leaves reliability, ordering, and congestion control to the application layer.

experiment.title: Run C POSIX UDP Echo & Multi-Datagram Experiments
experiment.instructions: Execute the compiled C POSIX UDP server and client (`examples/udp/`) under LD_PRELOAD socket tracing and libpcap UDP capture.
required_setup: Phase 2 LD_PRELOAD tracer and Phase 4 libpcap capture helper
execution_steps: Run 'Single UDP Datagram Echo' and verify there is NO connect/listen/accept and NO SYN/FIN packets.
Run 'Multiple Datagrams (Varied Payload Sizes)' and verify each message arrives intact with its exact byte length.
Run 'UDP Server Unavailable' to observe sendto() succeeding locally while recvfrom() times out.

supported_scenarios.label: 1. Single UDP Datagram Echo
supported_scenarios.description: C UDP client sends one datagram to localhost UDP server and receives the exact echoed datagram.

supported_scenarios.label: 2. Multiple Datagrams (Varied Payload Sizes)
supported_scenarios.description: Sends 4 distinct datagrams of sizes 5B, 28B, 64B, and 128B to demonstrate preserved datagram boundaries.

supported_scenarios.label: 3. UDP Server Unavailable (No Listener)
supported_scenarios.description: Sends a UDP datagram to an unbound localhost port; observes sendto() returning bytes sent while recvfrom() times out.

expected_observations: Socket API trace shows socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM), bind(), sendto(), recvfrom(), close() — zero listen()/accept().
Captured packets report protocol='UDP' with IPv4 header + 8-byte UDP header + exact datagram payload length.
Multiple datagrams stay separate 1-to-1 sendto/recvfrom operations.
observation_caveats: Because UDP has no SYN/FIN handshake, TCP flow handshake analysis does not apply to UDP runs.

questions.prompt: How many bytes is a standard UDP transport header?
options: 8 bytes (src port, dst port, length, checksum)
questions.rubric_summary: UDP headers are always fixed at 8 bytes.
questions.explanation: A UDP header contains four 16-bit fields: source port, destination port, length, and checksum — totaling exactly 8 bytes.

questions.prompt: A UDP client calls sendto() targeting an unbound port where no UDP server is running. What typically happens immediately on sendto()?
options: sendto() blocks until a server starts listening.
sendto() returns the byte count immediately because UDP is connectionless; failure only surfaces later via timeout or ICMP Port Unreachable.
The kernel performs a 3-way handshake and returns ECONNREFUSED on sendto().
The OS automatically starts an echo server.
questions.rubric_summary: UDP sendto() queues the datagram without verifying a peer listener.
questions.explanation: Because UDP performs no connection setup, sendto() hands the datagram to IP immediately; an unconnected UDP socket only sees unavailability when recvfrom() times out (or via ICMP error on connected UDP sockets).

questions.prompt: Compare how TCP and UDP handle message boundaries when an application performs two consecutive sends of 10 bytes and 20 bytes.
questions.rubric_summary: TCP is a byte stream (reads may coalesce/split); UDP preserves each datagram boundary.
questions.explanation: TCP treats data as an unstructured byte stream so one recv() might read 30 bytes or 15 bytes; UDP preserves message boundaries so each recvfrom() returns one discrete datagram (10 bytes, then 20 bytes).
